definitions.definition: Any woman who is, or has been, in a domestic relationship with the respondent and who alleges to have been subjected to any act of domestic violence by the respondent.
definitions.plain_english: An aggrieved person is a woman who is currently living with or has previously lived with a man in a close domestic relationship (such as a wife, partner, sister, mother, or daughter-in-law) and claims that he has subjected her to some form of domestic violence. This includes physical harm, emotional abuse, sexual abuse, or financial deprivation. She does not need to prove the abuse at the time of making the complaint — a mere allegation is sufficient to invoke the protections of the Act.
real_world_examples: A married woman in Mumbai whose husband regularly beats her and controls all household finances, preventing her from accessing money for basic needs, files a complaint under the Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act — she qualifies as an aggrieved person.

A woman in Delhi who was in a live-in relationship with a man for three years and was subjected to verbal abuse and threats, even after the relationship ended and she moved out, files an application for a protection order — she qualifies because she 'has been' in a domestic relationship.

A widowed mother-in-law in Chennai who is harassed and driven out of her matrimonial home by her son and daughter-in-law, where she has lived for decades, files a complaint alleging emotional and economic abuse — she qualifies as an aggrieved person as a family member in a shared household.

A woman in Kolkata whose husband's brother sexually assaults her while she is residing in a joint family home files a complaint against the brother-in-law — she is an aggrieved person seeking relief against a relative of the husband, as permitted by the proviso to the definition of 'respondent'.

A woman who left her abusive husband two years ago and now lives separately files an application for monetary relief for losses she suffered during the relationship — she qualifies because the definition covers women who 'have been' in a domestic relationship.

A woman in a relationship in the nature of marriage (long-term live-in partner) in Hyderabad whose partner throws her out of the shared household and stops providing financial support files a complaint — she is covered as an aggrieved person under the Act.
what_it_covers: A legally married wife who alleges any form of domestic violence by her husband.
A woman who was in a live-in relationship or a relationship in the nature of marriage and alleges domestic violence by her partner.
A mother, sister, daughter, or other female family member living in a joint family household who alleges domestic violence by a male member of that household.
A woman whose domestic relationship with the respondent has already ended (past relationship), provided she alleges she was subjected to domestic violence during that relationship.
A woman who alleges domestic violence by a relative of her husband or male partner, such as a brother-in-law or father-in-law, as enabled by the proviso to the definition of 'respondent'.
what_it_excludes: A man who claims to have been subjected to domestic violence — the definition is explicitly restricted to women only.
A woman who has no domestic relationship (whether current or past) with the respondent, such as a stranger or a purely professional acquaintance.
A woman who has been subjected to violence but does not allege that it was committed by the respondent with whom she shares or shared a domestic relationship.

A child (male or female) below eighteen years of age who suffers harm — they are not directly covered as an 'aggrieved person', though they may be protected incidentally through orders made in favour of the aggrieved person.
A woman who alleges violence by another woman, except where such complaint is directed against a female relative of the husband or male partner as permitted under the Act's proviso on respondents.

definitions.definition: "child" means any person below the age of eighteen years and includes any adopted, step or foster child.
definitions.plain_english: A 'child' under this law is anyone who is younger than 18 years old. This includes not just biological children but also children who have been legally adopted, stepchildren from a spouse's previous relationship, or children placed in foster care. The law uses this broad definition to ensure all children living in a domestic setting are protected regardless of their legal relationship to the adults.
real_world_examples: A 14-year-old biological son of the aggrieved woman living in the shared household is covered under this definition and can be included in a protection order sought by his mother against her abusive husband.

A 10-year-old girl adopted by a couple in Mumbai qualifies as a 'child' under this Act, and the aggrieved mother can seek a custody order under Section 21 to protect the adopted daughter from the abusive respondent.

A woman in Delhi who has a 16-year-old stepson from her husband's first marriage can seek relief under the Act that also covers the safety and custody arrangements of that stepchild, since he falls within the definition.

A foster child aged 8 living with a woman who is a victim of domestic violence in Chennai is included in this definition, entitling the Protection Officer to consider the child's welfare when filing a domestic incident report.

A 17-year-old daughter of an aggrieved woman in Kolkata who witnesses domestic abuse can be named in a protection order, and the court can restrict the respondent from contacting or approaching her under this definition.

A woman in Pune seeking monetary relief can specifically claim economic support for household necessities for her 12-year-old stepchild, as that child qualifies under this definition and is explicitly mentioned in the economic abuse provisions.
what_it_covers: Any biological child under 18 years of age living in or associated with the shared household of the aggrieved person.
A legally adopted child below 18 years, regardless of the duration or formality of the adoption process.
A stepchild below 18 years brought into the household through the spouse's previous relationship.
A foster child below 18 years placed in the care of the aggrieved person or the respondent.
A child below 18 years who is a subject of custody disputes arising from domestic violence proceedings under this Act.
what_it_excludes: Any person who has attained the age of 18 years or above, even if they are financially dependent on the aggrieved person or respondent.
An unborn child or foetus, as the definition explicitly requires a 'person' below eighteen years, implying live birth.
Adult children (aged 18 or above) of the aggrieved person, even if they are students or otherwise living in the shared household.
A ward or legal guardian relationship that does not constitute adoption, foster care, or step-parentage as generally understood under Indian law.
Children who are themselves respondents or adult parties in proceedings under this Act.

definitions.definition: Dependants, as used in the Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005, refers to persons who are financially, emotionally, or otherwise reliant upon the aggrieved person or the respondent, including children and other relatives who are under the care or support of either party and who may be subjected to violence as a means of coercing or harming the aggrieved person.
definitions.plain_english: Dependants are people who rely on either the victim or the accused for their daily needs, care, or support — such as children, elderly parents, or siblings living in the same household. The law protects them because an abuser might harm these individuals to intimidate or control the victim. Even though they are not the primary complainant, they are shielded under a protection order.
real_world_examples: A husband threatens to beat the couple's minor children unless his wife withdraws her domestic violence complaint — the children, as dependants, are protected under the protection order issued by the Magistrate.

A woman's elderly mother-in-law lives with her and is financially dependent on the household; the respondent threatens to throw her out of the home to pressure the aggrieved woman — the mother-in-law qualifies as a dependant deserving protection.

A respondent assaults his wife's younger sibling who lives with them and depends on the couple for education and shelter, using the assault as leverage against the aggrieved person — such a sibling is treated as a dependant under Section 18.

A woman's disabled brother who relies on her for daily care is threatened by her abusive spouse to prevent her from approaching authorities — the brother, being fully dependent on her, falls within the scope of dependants protected by a protection order.

In a joint family setup, a respondent threatens harm to the aggrieved person's young nephews and nieces who live in the shared household and depend on the family economically, to coerce her into silence — they are covered as dependants under the protection order.
what_it_covers: Minor children of the aggrieved person or the respondent who reside in the shared household and rely on either party for care and maintenance.
Elderly parents or in-laws who are financially or physically dependent on the aggrieved person or the respondent for daily sustenance and shelter.
Siblings, relatives, or other persons living in the shared household who depend on the aggrieved person for economic support or care and are targeted by the respondent to intimidate her.
Persons with physical or mental disabilities who are unable to support themselves and rely on the aggrieved person's household for survival.
Young relatives such as nephews, nieces, or wards in the care of the aggrieved person who could be used as instruments of pressure by the respondent.
what_it_excludes: Fully independent adult relatives who do not reside with or financially depend on either the aggrieved person or the respondent and have no reliance relationship with either party.

Friends or acquaintances of the aggrieved person who may assist her but do not have a dependency relationship — they are covered as 'other relatives or any person who gives assistance' rather than as dependants.
Strangers or neighbours with no familial, financial, or care-based connection to the aggrieved person or respondent, even if they are affected by acts of domestic violence.
The aggrieved person herself, who is separately defined and protected under the Act in her own capacity rather than as a dependant.
Respondent's independent adult children from a prior relationship who neither reside in the shared household nor depend on the aggrieved person for any form of support.
definitions.why_it_matters: If a person qualifies as a dependant, causing violence against them by the respondent is explicitly prohibited under a protection order issued under Section 18, making any such act a breach of the order and punishable under the Act. This definition is critical because it extends the protective reach of the Magistrate's order beyond just the aggrieved person, preventing the respondent from using harm to third parties as a tool of coercion or control.

definitions.definition: "domestic incident report" means a report made in the prescribed form on receipt of a complaint of domestic violence from an aggrieved person.
definitions.plain_english: A domestic incident report is an official written record prepared by a Protection Officer when a woman complains about domestic violence. It is filled out in a government-prescribed format and documents the details of the complaint. This report is then forwarded to the Magistrate, the local police station, and relevant service providers so that appropriate action can be taken.
real_world_examples: A woman in Delhi reports to the Protection Officer that her husband has been beating her regularly; the Protection Officer fills out the prescribed form capturing details of the violence, the parties involved, and the circumstances, thereby creating a domestic incident report.

A wife in Mumbai alleges that her in-laws have locked her out of the shared household and seized her stridhan; the Protection Officer records all these facts in the prescribed form and forwards copies to the local police station and nearby shelter home service providers.

An aggrieved woman in Chennai approaches a registered service provider (NGO) about ongoing economic abuse by her husband who has cut off all financial support; the NGO assists in making the domestic incident report which is then submitted to the Magistrate to initiate proceedings.

A woman in Kolkata who has suffered verbal and emotional abuse for years finally approaches the Protection Officer; the Officer prepares the domestic incident report in the prescribed form and forwards it to the Magistrate under Section 9 to enable the court to take cognizance of the complaint and issue directions.

During a counselling session at a government welfare office in Pune, a woman discloses physical abuse by her spouse; the Protection Officer on duty prepares the domestic incident report and simultaneously informs the police station having jurisdiction over the area where the violence occurred.
what_it_covers: A report made in the prescribed government form recording a complaint of domestic violence received from an aggrieved woman by the Protection Officer.
Details of the alleged domestic violence incident including nature of abuse, parties involved, and the shared household, as documented upon receipt of the complaint.
Reports prepared by Protection Officers under Section 9 that are forwarded to the Magistrate, the jurisdictional police station, and service providers in the area.
Reports that may be initiated through a registered service provider under Section 10, who is also empowered to record and forward such reports.
The document that serves as the formal basis for the Magistrate to take cognizance of the complaint and issue directions under Sections 12 and 24.
what_it_excludes: Informal oral or written complaints made directly to police under the IPC or CrPC that do not use the prescribed DV Act form — such complaints do not constitute a domestic incident report under this Act.
Medical or injury reports prepared by doctors or medical facilities about injuries sustained by the aggrieved person, even if related to domestic violence — these are separate documents.
Complaints or reports filed by persons who are not 'aggrieved persons' as defined under the Act, such as complaints by adult male family members or third parties who are not the victim.
Reports or records maintained internally by shelter homes or NGOs that are not forwarded to the Magistrate in the prescribed format.
Police FIRs or charge sheets filed under criminal law provisions — these are distinct legal documents governed by the CrPC, not the DV Act.
definitions.why_it_matters: The domestic incident report is the foundational procedural document that formally initiates relief proceedings under the Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005 — its submission to the Magistrate under Sections 9 and 12 triggers the court's jurisdiction to grant protection orders, residence orders, monetary relief, and custody orders. Without a domestic incident report being filed in the prescribed form, the Protection Officer's statutory duty under Section 9 is not discharged, and the Magistrate's ability to take cognizance and issue interim or final orders under Sections 12 and 24 may be compromised.

definitions.definition: "domestic relationship" means a relationship between two persons who live or have, at any point of time, lived together in a shared household, when they are related by consanguinity, marriage, or through a relationship in the nature of marriage, adoption or are family members living together as a joint family.
definitions.plain_english: A domestic relationship is a connection between two people who currently live together or have previously lived together in the same home. This connection can arise through blood ties, marriage, a live-in relationship similar to marriage, adoption, or being part of the same joint family. The law uses this definition to decide who can seek protection under the Domestic Violence Act.
real_world_examples: A married woman living with her husband and in-laws in a shared household in Mumbai — the relationship between her and her husband, as well as her in-laws, qualifies as a domestic relationship, making her eligible to file a complaint under the Act.

A woman who has been living with a man as his partner without formal marriage (live-in relationship) in Delhi for three years — their relationship 'in the nature of marriage' constitutes a domestic relationship, entitling her to seek protection orders.

An adult daughter living with her parents and siblings in a joint family home in Chennai — her relationship with all family members in that household is a domestic relationship, even if she later moves out, as the Act covers past cohabitation.

A woman who was previously married and lived with her husband in Kolkata but is now separated — despite no longer living together, the past shared residence means the domestic relationship still legally exists for the purpose of filing a complaint.

A woman adopted into a family and living with her adoptive parents and siblings in a shared household in Hyderabad — the adoptive relationship qualifies as a domestic relationship under the Act, covering acts of violence by any family member.

A widowed sister-in-law continuing to reside in the joint family home of her deceased husband's family in Jaipur — her cohabitation with the joint family members establishes a domestic relationship with each of them for the purposes of the Act.
what_it_covers: A legally married couple currently or previously residing together in a shared household.
A man and woman in a live-in or cohabiting relationship 'in the nature of marriage,' even without formal solemnization.
Members of a joint Hindu family or other joint family structures living or having lived together, including siblings, parents, in-laws, and other relatives.
An adopted child and their adoptive family members residing in the same household.
A woman who has separated or divorced but previously shared the household — past cohabitation is sufficient to establish the relationship.
what_it_excludes: Two persons who are related by blood or marriage but have never lived together in a shared household at any point in time.
A purely romantic or intimate relationship where the parties have never cohabited — there must be actual shared residence at some stage.
Roommates or paying guests sharing a residence purely for commercial or convenience purposes without any familial, marital, or adoptive connection.
Relationships between an aggrieved person and a third party who is not connected through consanguinity, marriage, adoption, or joint family living arrangements.
definitions.why_it_matters: The existence of a 'domestic relationship' is a jurisdictional prerequisite under the Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005 — an aggrieved person can only seek relief such as protection orders (Section 18), residence orders (Section 19), or monetary relief if she is or has been in a domestic relationship with the respondent. If this definition does not apply, the Magistrate has no power to entertain the complaint or grant any remedy under the Act.

definitions.definition: "Dowry" shall have the same meaning as assigned to it in section 2 of the Dowry Prohibition Act, 1961 (28 of 1961), which defines it as any property or valuable security given or agreed to be given either directly or indirectly by one party to a marriage to the other party, or by the parents of either party to a marriage or by any other person, to either party to the marriage or to any other person, at or before or any time after the marriage in connection with the marriage of the said parties.
definitions.plain_english: Dowry refers to money, property, jewellery, goods, or any other valuables that are given or promised by one side of a marriage (usually the bride's family) to the other side (usually the groom or his family), in connection with the marriage. It does not matter who physically gives it — parents, relatives, or anyone else acting in connection with the marriage.
real_world_examples: A bride's parents in Uttar Pradesh hand over cash, gold jewellery, and a car to the groom's family on the day of the wedding as part of a pre-agreed settlement — this constitutes dowry under the Act.

A groom's family in Tamil Nadu demands that the bride's parents pay a lump sum amount and purchase household appliances after the wedding, threatening to harass the wife if not complied with — such post-marriage demands for property in connection with the marriage amount to unlawful dowry demands.

A Maharashtra family agrees before the engagement that the bride's brother will transfer agricultural land to the groom as a condition of the marriage proceeding — this property transfer, even if done indirectly through a relative, qualifies as dowry.

A groom's parents in Delhi repeatedly pressure their daughter-in-law to bring more gold and a scooter from her parents, citing that other families in their community gave more — such coercive demands for additional property post-marriage constitute harassment related to dowry under the DV Act.

A bride's family in Rajasthan gifts a refrigerator, furniture, and fixed deposit receipts to the groom's family as part of customary exchange during the wedding ceremony — even if framed as a 'gift', these qualify as dowry as they are given in connection with the marriage.

Valuable securities such as fixed deposits, shares, or bonds transferred by any person to either party in connection with the marriage.
Indirect transfers made through parents, relatives, or third parties on behalf of either party to the marriage, as long as they are connected to the marriage.
Post-marriage demands for additional property or valuables made by the groom's family that are linked to the marriage agreement.
Gifts or transfers framed as 'customary' or 'voluntary' but given under social pressure or as a precondition of the marriage.
what_it_excludes: Stridhan — property, gifts, or money given to the woman herself (the bride) as her personal property, which she retains full ownership and control over.
Voluntary gifts given to the bride or groom by relatives at the time of marriage that are not connected to any demand or condition of the marriage.
Dower or Mahr in Muslim marriages, which is a mandatory payment from the groom to the bride and is governed separately under personal law.

definitions.plain_english: Economic abuse means any action by the respondent that controls, withholds, or destroys the woman's access to money, property, or financial resources she needs or is legally entitled to. It includes stopping her from using shared assets, selling off her belongings without her consent, or preventing her from accessing the family home or household facilities. The purpose of recognising this as abuse is to protect women from being made financially helpless or dependent as a form of control.
real_world_examples: A husband in Delhi refuses to give his wife any household money for groceries, medicines, or school fees for their children, forcing her into complete financial dependence and inability to meet daily needs.
A man sells his wife's gold jewellery and stridhan items (gifted to her at marriage) without her knowledge or consent, and transfers the proceeds to his own personal bank account.
A mother-in-law in Mumbai changes the locks of the shared household and denies the daughter-in-law entry, effectively cutting off her access to the shared home and all household facilities.
A husband in Chennai stops paying the rent for the house where his wife lives separately after a dispute, intending to force her out by having her evicted due to non-payment.

A respondent in Kolkata transfers jointly held shares, fixed deposits, and immovable property entirely into his own name or that of relatives to prevent his wife from claiming any stake in matrimonial assets.
A husband withholds court-ordered maintenance payments for months and simultaneously prevents his wife from taking up employment by confiscating her educational certificates and identity documents.

Selling, transferring, or alienating the aggrieved person's stridhan, jointly held property, shares, securities, or other movable and immovable assets without her consent.
Blocking or restricting the aggrieved person's access to the shared household or to facilities and resources she is entitled to use by virtue of the domestic relationship.
Failure to pay court-ordered or customary maintenance amounts to the aggrieved person.
Preventing the aggrieved person from using or benefiting from property or assets in which she has a legal or equitable interest arising from the domestic relationship.

Mutual, consensual financial decisions taken jointly by both parties regarding shared assets or household expenses.
Financial disputes or property claims between strangers or parties who do not share a domestic relationship as defined under the Act.
Civil or commercial debt recovery actions by third-party creditors against the respondent that incidentally reduce assets available to the aggrieved person.
Temporary or incidental delays in making payments that are not part of a pattern of coercive financial control directed at the aggrieved person.

definitions.definition: An interim protection order is a temporary order passed by a Magistrate under the Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005, granted on an ex parte basis pending the final hearing and disposal of an application for a protection order, for the purpose of protecting an aggrieved person from domestic violence. A breach of such an interim protection order by the respondent constitutes a punishable offence under Section 31 of the Act.
definitions.plain_english: An interim protection order is a short-term, emergency court order that a judge can issue quickly — even before hearing the other side — to protect a woman from domestic violence while her main case is still being decided. It acts as an immediate shield, stopping the abuser from committing further violence, contacting her, or entering her home. Violating this order is a criminal offence and can result in jail time or a fine.
real_world_examples: A woman in Mumbai files a complaint against her husband for physical assault. The Magistrate, without waiting for a full hearing, immediately issues an interim protection order directing the husband not to enter the matrimonial home or contact the wife until the case is decided.

A woman in Delhi is being harassed and threatened by her in-laws. The Magistrate passes an interim protection order prohibiting the in-laws from visiting her workplace or sending her threatening messages, providing immediate relief before the main protection order hearing.

A woman in Chennai who has fled to her parents' home with her children obtains an interim protection order from the local Magistrate preventing her husband from taking the children away or approaching her parents' residence during the pendency of the case.

In Kolkata, a woman reports continuous economic abuse where her husband has locked her out of their joint bank accounts. The Magistrate issues an interim protection order restraining the husband from alienating or disposing of any shared household assets until the case is resolved.

A woman in Bengaluru who faces repeated verbal threats and intimidation from her live-in partner obtains an interim protection order directing the respondent to maintain a specified distance from her and refrain from communication through any medium while the case is heard.
what_it_covers: Orders passed by a Magistrate on an urgent or ex parte basis restraining the respondent from committing acts of domestic violence against the aggrieved person, before the final disposal of the main application.

Any short-term judicial directive aimed at protecting the aggrieved person from physical abuse, sexual abuse, verbal and emotional abuse, or economic abuse while the protection order application is pending before the court.

Violations of such an interim protection order by the respondent, which are treated as criminal offences punishable with imprisonment up to one year or fine up to twenty thousand rupees or both under Section 31.
what_it_excludes: A final or permanent protection order issued after full hearing of both parties, which is governed separately and referred to distinctly as a 'protection order' under the Act.

Orders passed by authorities other than a Magistrate, such as administrative directions issued by a Protection Officer or instructions given by a service provider, which do not carry the same legal enforceability as an interim protection order.

Civil injunctions or restraining orders passed by a civil court under the Civil Procedure Code in matrimonial or property disputes, which are not interim protection orders under the Domestic Violence Act.
Maintenance or monetary relief orders issued on an interim basis, which are separate from interim protection orders and do not fall within the scope of Section 31 of this Act.

A woman living in Mumbai (a metropolitan city) files a complaint against her husband under the DV Act; the Metropolitan Magistrate at the family court in Mumbai exercises jurisdiction as the 'Magistrate' and issues an ex-parte interim protection order.

A woman who has fled domestic violence in Chennai and is temporarily staying at a shelter home in Bengaluru files her complaint before the JMFC in Bengaluru, which qualifies as the competent Magistrate because the aggrieved person 'resides temporarily' within that jurisdiction.

A Protection Officer in Delhi submits a domestic incident report to the Metropolitan Magistrate of the area where the respondent husband resides, and that Magistrate proceeds to take cognizance and summon the respondent as required under Section 13.

A woman from a rural district in Rajasthan alleges domestic violence committed in her matrimonial home; the Judicial Magistrate First Class of that district is the competent Magistrate because the domestic violence is alleged to have taken place within that territorial jurisdiction.

Under this law, if a husband or his family takes away, sells, or blocks her access to her stridhan, that act is treated as a form of domestic violence called economic abuse.

Household items, clothes, utensils, and other valuables received as wedding gifts that form part of the woman's personal estate.

Examples: A husband repeatedly calls his wife 'barren' and insults her in front of family members because she has not conceived a child after two years of marriage, causing her severe emotional distress. | A mother-in-law routinely mocks and ridicules her daughter-in-law for giving birth to a girl child, calling her 'inauspicious' and 'a burden', and making derogatory remarks about her family. | A husband regularly threatens his wife that he will harm her parents or siblings if she does not comply with his demands, causing her to live in constant fear. | A spouse calls his wife humiliating names in front of their children and guests, degrades her intelligence and appearance on a daily basis, and dismisses her opinions with contempt and ridicule. | An aggrieved woman's husband tells her repeatedly during arguments that he will 'make her pay' and will hurt her brother, using these threats as a tool of psychological control over her behaviour. | A woman is consistently mocked by her husband and in-laws for coming from a lower economic background, with daily taunts and name-calling designed to make her feel inferior and worthless.

Covers: Insults and ridicule directed at the aggrieved person specifically regarding her inability to conceive or her failure to produce a male child.; Name calling, humiliation, and demeaning remarks made towards the aggrieved person in private or in the presence of others.; Repeated threats made by the respondent to cause physical pain to any person — such as the woman's parents, children, or siblings — in whom the aggrieved person has an emotional interest.; Systematic ridicule and mockery of the aggrieved person's character, appearance, family background, or personal choices designed to demean her self-worth.; Verbal conduct that, though not physical, endangers the mental well-being of the aggrieved person within the scope of domestic violence under Section 3.

Excludes: Acts of physical force, assault, or criminal intimidation causing bodily harm, which fall under 'physical abuse' as defined separately in Section 3(i).; Sexual conduct that abuses or degrades the woman, which is separately governed by the definition of 'sexual abuse' under Section 3(ii).; Economic deprivation, disposal of assets, or restriction of financial resources, which are exclusively covered under 'economic abuse' as defined in Section 3(iv).; A single, isolated, or one-time remark or threat that lacks a pattern of repetition, as the definition implies ongoing or repeated conduct, particularly for threats.; Verbal disputes or heated arguments between strangers or non-domestic parties, as the definition applies only within the context of a domestic relationship between the respondent and the aggrieved person.

Why it matters: If an act qualifies as verbal and emotional abuse under Section 3, it constitutes 'domestic violence' under the Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005, enabling the aggrieved person to apply for a protection order, residence order, and monetary relief, and obligating Protection Officers and Magistrates to act on a domestic incident report. Failure to establish this definition means the conduct may not trigger the statutory remedies and emergency reliefs available under the Act.
